name: GHRP-5
lead: GHRP-5 is a synthetic growth hormone-releasing peptide, also called the Momany peptide, that belongs to the family of ghrelin-receptor agonists. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding settings, growth hormone secretagogues are discussed for a chain of effects people hope for: more growth hormone and IGF-1 signalling, which they associate with leaner body composition, muscle growth and recovery, and with a more muscular, defined physique. A 2026 review notes that growth hormone-releasing peptides have been used by amateur sportsmen and bodybuilders.[2] Analytical papers group GHRP-5 with GHRP-1, -2, -4 and -6 as synthetic met-enkephalin analogues containing unnatural D-amino acids and designed to stimulate growth hormone release.[4]

Published work on GHRP-5 itself is limited to laboratory studies in rats and cell cultures, anti-doping chemistry and peptide-handling studies. A rat study reported that acute and chronic GHRP-5 administration released growth hormone, and a second study examined its prolactin-releasing activity on lactotroph cells.[1][5] No human clinical studies of GHRP-5 were found.
GHRP-5 is not an approved medicine. It appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list of prohibited peptides and is covered by urine screening methods used in sport.[6][7]

chain: Binds the ghrelin / growth hormone secretagogue receptor
Claimed: higher GH and IGF-1 signalling supporting leaner, more muscular physique
angle.text: Users of growth hormone secretagogues generally cite fat loss, muscle fullness, recovery and skin or sleep benefits as the aims. For GHRP-5 specifically, these outcomes have been described only as claims, since the published work consists of laboratory and analytical studies.

GHRH analogues such as sermorelin and tesamorelin [3]

paras: Interest in GHRP-5 follows the logic of the wider secretagogue family. Growth hormone and IGF-1 signalling are associated with lean mass and fat distribution, so people pursuing a more muscular or leaner physique look to peptides that raise GH release as an alternative route to injecting growth hormone itself. Wikipedia states that the main clinical application of growth hormone secretagogues is treating growth hormone deficiency, and that many also raise IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol [3]. GHRP-5 has no approved use, and the research on it is limited to the laboratory findings described below.

GHRP-5 is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR). Wikipedia's page on growth hormone secretagogues lists GHRP-1 through GHRP-6 among the GHSR agonists, separate from agents such as sermorelin and tesamorelin that act at the GHRH receptor.[3] Many secretagogues also raise IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol.[3]

A study in the Histochemical Journal examined the somatotroph cell population of rats under GHRP-5 treatment. Acute and chronic administration provoked a significant release of growth hormone linked to ultrastructural changes in pituitary somatotrophs. After 14 days, pituitary growth hormone content fell as serum GH peaked, and cell culture experiments with pathway blockers indicated that the phospholipase C-inositol phosphate system was involved.[1]

In a Biocell study, daily GHRP-5 treatment of male rats for three days did not significantly change serum prolactin, whereas adding it to pituitary cell cultures significantly increased prolactin release, about 50 percent above untreated controls in cultures enriched with lactotrophs. The treatment also changed the fine structure of lactotroph cells in ways consistent with increased secretory activity.[5]

A 2026 study in Chirality examined the secondary structure, thermal stability and model-membrane interactions of growth hormone-releasing peptides, and a 2023 study characterised the enzymatic and serum stability of doping-related peptides including GHRP-4, GHRP-5 and GHRP-6.[2][9] A 2017 paper used GHRP-5 as one of four doping-relevant model peptides in an analysis of peptide adsorption to laboratory surfaces.[11]

The receptor that GHRPs act on is the one whose natural ligand is ghrelin. Kojima and colleagues described ghrelin in 1999 as a growth-hormone-releasing acylated peptide from the stomach, and Wikipedia reports that it is best known as the hunger hormone, with levels peaking before meals, and that its receptor, GHS-R1a, mediates GH release along with increased hunger [14]. This shared receptor is why the peptide family is often described in community discussion as affecting appetite as well as GH, although appetite effects of GHRP-5 specifically have not been reported in the studies found.

Wikipedia's page on GHRP-6, a better-characterised family member, says that simultaneous insulin increases the GH response to that peptide and that carbohydrate or fat around the time of administration markedly blunts GH release; these observations belong to GHRP-6 and have not been tested for GHRP-5 [12].

Wikipedia notes that GHRP-6 is a synthetic met-enkephalin analogue without opioid activity that potently stimulates GH release through the ghrelin receptor; it has an oral bioavailability under 1 percent and an elimination half-life of about 2.5 hours.[12] These GHRP-6 properties are reported on its own page and have not been measured for GHRP-5.

Anti-doping laboratories have published urine screening methods covering GHRP-5. A 2014 LC-MS/MS method for equine and human urine, a 2016 direct-injection ion-mobility screen and a 2011 liquid chromatography study all included it among the peptides they detect.[4][6][7] The peptides are described as orally active, and the established growth hormone test does not detect their use, which is why separate screens were developed.[7]
The 2016 paper lists GHRP-5 among peptides under 2 kDa on the WADA prohibited list, together with GHRP-1, -2, -3, -4, -6, hexarelin, ipamorelin, TB-500 and others.[6]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Community discussion of growth hormone-releasing peptides centres more often on GHRP-6, GHRP-2, ipamorelin and hexarelin than on GHRP-5. Forum users describe the family as a way to raise growth hormone for fat loss and muscle gain. Specific dose, cycling and sourcing practices are not described here.

GHRP-5 is not approved by regulators as a medicine. Anti-doping laboratories screen for it because it is on the WADA prohibited list, and published methods exist for detecting it in equine and human urine [4][6][7]. Wikipedia places GHRP-6, its relative, among WADA-prohibited substances [12].
No studies found. Growth hormone secretagogues as a class have human data, for example GHRP-6 studied in patients with insulin-dependent diabetes, but those studies concern other peptides.[13]

The only laboratory work on GHRP-5 itself comes from two rat and cell-culture studies of pituitary GH and prolactin release and from analytical and stability studies [1][5][9][11]. Wikipedia's GHRP-6 page notes a study in normal mice reporting differences in body composition, muscle growth, glucose metabolism, memory and cardiac function, but this concerns GHRP-6 [12].

card.summary: The "Momany peptide": a GH-releasing peptide with lab and anti-doping papers but no human trials.
card.note: Prohibited in competitive sport; no human clinical studies found.

quick.overview:
GHRP-5 is a synthetic peptide in the growth hormone-releasing peptide family, also called the Momany peptide, and is discussed in muscle-building contexts.

The literature is limited to anti-doping chemistry and a few laboratory studies. No human clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: It is classed as an agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor, and one laboratory study reported it also releases prolactin.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list and is not an approved medicine.
